description: We’re Shadowline, final-year CS students from FAST-NUCES Karachi, building for the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser challenge. Our app lets anyone pick a landing site and dates at the Moon’s south pole and instantly see when the Sun is up (power) and when Earth is visible (comms). Existing tools are built for specialists; we want it quick and clear for everyone. We’re a backend, data and AI team, currently building a decentralized AI fact-checking network as our FYP.
summary:
Shadowline is a web app that helps mission planners, teachers and students decide where and when to land on the Moon. You pick a landing site and a date, and it shows where the Sun and Earth are in that site's sky compared to the real hills around it. That tells you when a lander would have sunlight for power and when it could talk to Earth.

The Sun and Earth positions come from NASA JPL data, and we checked our results against JPL Horizons. The hills around each site come from NASA LOLA elevation maps. The app shows how much of the mission gets sunlight and Earth contact, how long until sunset or Earthset, the longest dark period, and an overall verdict. You can compare sites, find the best landing dates if a launch is delayed, and explore the Moon and the ground around a site in 3D.

This matters most at the south pole, where the Sun stays very low. At Shackleton ridge in February 2027, a model that assumes flat ground says the site gets no sunlight at all. With the real terrain it gets sunlight 80.7% of the time. Getting the terrain right can decide whether a mission survives.
details:
What it does

Shadowline helps people choose where and when to land on the Moon. You pick a landing site (11 real sites from Apollo 11 to future CLPS targets, or any coordinates) and a date, and the app shows where the Sun and Earth are in that site's sky compared to the real hills around it. From that it works out how much of the mission has sunlight for power, how much of the time the lander can talk to Earth, the longest dark stretch, countdowns to the next sunset and Earthset, and a simple verdict: good, risky or not viable.

How it works

We calculate Sun and Earth positions with Skyfield using NASA JPL's DE421 ephemeris and lunar orientation files, so the Moon's wobble (libration) is included. We checked our results against JPL Horizons at four sites and the largest difference was 0.04 arcseconds. For terrain we used NASA LOLA elevation maps. For every site we look out in 360 directions up to 150 km, account for the Moon's curve, and save the real skyline. At every moment the app checks whether the Sun and Earth are above that skyline, even when the Sun is only partly hidden.

Benefits and impact

Today, checking one site and date means using several specialist tools. Shadowline puts the answer on one screen. Planners can compare sites and dates side by side, and when a launch slips, the best dates tool scans months of start times and lists the next good landing windows. Every view is a shareable link, so science and engineering teams look at the same result. A simple mode and a learn page explain the south pole problem for students and the public, while an expert mode gives exact numbers and CSV downloads.

What makes it creative

The sky plot switches to a panorama view at the poles, where everything happens a few degrees above the horizon. A 3D Moon is lit by the real Sun and shows where Earth can be seen, and a 3D terrain view shows real shadows moving across the ground, including a view from the lander itself. Our most striking result: at Shackleton ridge in February 2027 the Sun never rises above a flat horizon, so a flat ground model says zero sunlight. With real terrain the ridge is lit 80.7% of the time.

Tools

Python, FastAPI, Skyfield, NumPy and rasterio on the backend. Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind, Three.js and React Three Fiber on the frontend. Playwright and pytest for testing. Hosted on Render and Vercel. We used Claude Code as a coding assistant throughout the project.

What we considered

Accuracy came first, so we validated against JPL Horizons and corrected a small offset between two NASA map frames. We were honest about limits: custom points use a flat horizon and the app says so, and our verdict thresholds are our own choices that can be adjusted. We also made it fast, usable on phones, accessible, and able to wake up gracefully on free hosting.
